solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Venomous types given firm support by Society

parts.note: Co is the usual abbreviation for company, a firm
a bra is an undergarment that gives support

explanation.surface: Poisonous creatures are being propped up by some institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given ... by' simply joins the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: These snakes are well known for their poisonous bite, so they are venomous types of animal.

clue.text: Nothing wrong with activity involving tricks — part of the British Establishment!

parts.note: the round letter O stands for zero or nothing
a cross mark X shows that something is wrong
bridge is a card game in which players win tricks

explanation.surface: A claim that a pastime of conjuring tricks is perfectly acceptable to the upper crust.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'tricks' are not conjuring but the tricks taken in the card game bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford and Cambridge universities together are seen as a pillar of the British ruling class.

clue.text: He drifts off — light going explains it

indicators.note: off suggests the letters have gone wrong or awry, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A man nods off to sleep as the lights go out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is someone dozing as the light fades; the definition is the astronomer's explanation for light from receding galaxies.
explanation.definitionFit: A shift of light towards longer wavelengths shows that its source is moving away, so receding light explains the effect.

clue.text: Tiny Devon village that is regarded as unimportant

parts.note: tiny means small
Beer is a fishing village on the coast of Devon, a county in south-west England

explanation.surface: A little hamlet in Devon is thought to be of no consequence.
explanation.walkthrough: BEER is a village on the Devon coast in south-west England, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Small beer is an idiom for a trivial matter, something of little importance.

clue.text: It's 'zythum' — that's a definitive statement

definitions.meaning: zythum, an ancient Egyptian malt beer, comes at the very end of many English dictionaries
a final authoritative pronouncement that settles an argument

explanation.surface: An obscure word for an ancient beer is held up as the final say on the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Zythum is famous for being the closing entry of many dictionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both the final entry in a list of words and the conclusive remark in a debate.

clue.text: As zeal misfires, I change to a policy of non-interference

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the preceding letters

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An official, seeing enthusiasm backfire, switches to a hands-off approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misfires' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'change' does the job.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine of leaving markets and people alone without government intervention is exactly a hands-off policy.

clue.text: A day in Herts town doing business

indicators.note: in places the first pieces inside the town's name

parts.note: Tring is a market town in Hertfordshire (Herts), a county north of London

explanation.surface: Someone spends a day in a Hertfordshire town on business.
explanation.walkthrough: TRING is a small town in Hertfordshire, a county just north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading is buying and selling, which is carrying on business.

clue.text: Some ghost in a town making a series of musical sounds

definitions.text: making a series of musical sounds

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A phantom haunting a town is producing eerie noises.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostinato is a short musical phrase repeated persistently, a recurring pattern of notes.

clue.text: Raving Greek character, one annoyed, upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the run of letters is turned upside down, so read from bottom to top

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
the Roman numeral I is one
annoyed means riled

explanation.surface: A Greek man is ranting, irritated and agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the whole run MUIRILED, which read the other way round gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Delirium is a state of wild confused excitement, so raving in the noun sense is a fair swap.

clue.text: A pal met with familiarity, no end, in port

parts.note: bud is American slang for a friend or pal

indicators.note: no end tells us to drop the final letter of the word

parts.note: a habit is something familiar through repetition

explanation.surface: Meeting a friend with easy informality at a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' strips the last letter from HABIT to leave HABI.
explanation.definitionFit: This emirate's capital on the Persian Gulf is a major seaport.

clue.text: Drawing line at the edge of doughy mass

indicators.note: at the edge of places the line letter on the outer end of the other piece

parts.note: paste is a soft doughy mixture

explanation.surface: Sketching a line around the rim of a lump of dough.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastel is a drawing made with chalky crayons of the same name.

clue.text: Saint as lion out to protect church

indicators.note: to protect means one piece wraps around and shields the other
out suggests the letters are disordered and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A holy figure, lion-like, goes out to defend the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges AS LION into NIOLAS, and 'to protect' wraps those letters around CH.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Nicholas, the bishop of Myra, is a famous saint and the model for Santa Claus.

clue.text: Victor or Michael?

definitions.meaning: a victor is one who wins a contest
Michael ... was an English film director, known for the Death Wish films

explanation.surface: A man's name, perhaps Victor or perhaps Michael.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor looks like a first name alongside Michael, but it is the common noun for a champion.
explanation.definitionFit: A victor is someone who triumphs, and Michael Winner was a well-known British film-maker bearing that surname.

clue.text: Cold can give you unlimited appetite

parts.note: free means without limit or restriction
zing is zest or keen enthusiasm, an appetite for life

explanation.surface: A chilly spell can leave you with a boundless hunger.
explanation.definitionFit: Freezing describes something extremely cold, at or below the temperature at which water turns to ice.

clue.text: Drunk hitting me when it's dark

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters are staggering about and out of order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An inebriated person strikes me after dark.
explanation.definitionFit: The hours between sunset and sunrise are the period of darkness.

clue.text: Do nothing, being in dire straits

indicators.note: being in says the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning their junction

explanation.surface: Advice to stay idle when in terrible difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: To rest is to stop working and remain idle, which is doing nothing.

clue.text: Agitated rector, I may get hot inside, producing empty verbiage

indicators.note: inside means one piece is placed within the other
agitated means stirred up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A flustered clergyman, overheated, delivers a meaningless sermon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agitated' rearranges RECTOR and I into RETORIC, and 'inside' puts H within it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhetoric used dismissively means grand language lacking real substance or sincerity.

clue.text: Airbus flying over British university's residential parts?

indicators.note: over means one piece is spread across and encloses the other
flying suggests the letters are in motion and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange
U is an abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An aircraft passes above a British campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' rearranges AIRBUS into SURBIA, and 'over' sets it around B and U.
explanation.definitionFit: The suburbs are the largely residential districts on the outskirts of a city, so a question mark flags the loose phrasing.

clue.text: Sound of swirling crowd gathering round

indicators.note: gathering means one piece collects the other inside it
swirling means the word is turned round and read the other way

parts.note: a mob is an unruly crowd
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: The noise made by a churning throng closing in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirling' turns MOB into BOM, and 'gathering' takes O inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A boom is a deep resonant noise, such as thunder or a cannon.

clue.text: Spooner's eager budgie, say, gets food

indicators.note: Spooner's signals that the opening sounds of two words are swapped

parts.note: keen means eager
a budgie is an example of a bird

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic pet budgerigar is given its feed.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first sounds of KEEN and BIRD gives BEAN and CURD.
explanation.definitionFit: Bean curd, or tofu, is a soft food made from soya milk.

clue.text: Item that's yellow — 'butter', might you say?

parts.note: an object is a thing or item
or is the heraldic term for gold or yellow

explanation.surface: Something golden-coloured, perhaps a pat of butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' suggests the dairy spread; read it as one who butts, raising objections.
explanation.definitionFit: An objector who keeps butting in could jokingly be called a butter, one who butts.

clue.text: Shape of infantrymen getting into mess

indicators.note: getting into means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a tangle is a muddle or mess
RI is the Royal Irish Regiment, an infantry regiment

explanation.surface: The state of foot soldiers after blundering into chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' suggests a military dining room, fitting the soldiers, but here it is a muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle is a geometric figure with three sides.

clue.text: Line traversed by metropolitan gentlemen

indicators.note: traversed by says the answer is crossed by the words, lying inside them

explanation.surface: A route crossed by city gents.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at a single point.

clue.text: Loyal worker, not English shirker

indicators.note: not English tells us to remove the letter E, its abbreviation

parts.note: true means loyal or faithful
an ant is the classic example of a worker insect

explanation.surface: A faithful employee who is not English dodges work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not English' removes E from TRUE, leaving TRU.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant stays away from school or duty without leave, which is shirking.

clue.text: Reunites different groups trailing behind

indicators.note: different means the letters are made into something else by rearranging

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Bringing together several separate parties that follow on.
explanation.definitionFit: Retinues are bodies of attendants following an important person.

clue.text: Disease running rampant in Serbia

indicators.note: running rampant means out of control, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An illness spreading unchecked through a Balkan country.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabies is a viral illness spread by animal bites.

clue.text: Wrongdoing at home I give up before start of year

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in
quit means to give up

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone at home vows to give up a vice before the new year.
explanation.definitionFit: Iniquity is immoral or grossly unfair behaviour, a sin.

clue.text: Reform movement has endless sort of magnetism — time to get stuck in

indicators.note: to get stuck in means the piece is pushed inside the other
endless tells us to drop the last letter

parts.note: charisma is personal magnetism

explanation.surface: A political campaign possessing a charm that never ends, waiting for its moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts CHARISMA to CHARISM, and 'to get stuck in' puts T inside it. Chartism was a 19th-century British working-class campaign for voting rights.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartism was a 1830s-1850s British campaign pressing for parliamentary reforms such as universal male suffrage.

clue.text: Bear close by river

parts.note: close means end, as of a day
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, northern England

explanation.surface: A bear sits near the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a favourite in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure is to tolerate or put up with something, the verb sense of bear.
